notes.coinbase_maturity: The size of the maturity ring, indexed by height modulo this value. Zero divides by zero inside the fold on every block (I1-L11).
notes.emission_decay_divisor: One part per epoch, the same divisor mainnet uses — but a devnet epoch is 64 blocks at 5 s, about 5.3 minutes, so the curve runs roughly 270x faster than mainnet's and reaches the tail in about 16 days rather than about twelve years. That is the point of a devnet — the emission schedule is reachable in a test run — and it is why this note does not repeat mainnet's 'halves every two years', which is a statement about mainnet's epoch length and not about this divisor.
notes.treasury_share_bps: The fraction of every block subsidy credited to the treasury cell (whitepaper 14.1), the remainder paying consensus. On the subsidy only, never on fees. The floor goes to the treasury and the remainder to the producer, so the two always sum to the subsidy exactly.
notes.pow_engine: dev-blake3, so a binary built WITHOUT the randomx tag runs this network. A binary built WITH the tag runs it too, and the asymmetry is deliberate rather than an oversight: pow.Dev is compiled unconditionally, so a tagged binary genuinely holds both engines and verifies this network correctly. Refusing it would buy no safety and would cost a second binary for anyone testing both networks. THE SAFETY PROPERTY IS ONE-DIRECTIONAL and it is the direction that can lose money: a binary lacking RandomX must never run a RandomX network, because with no engine to fall back to except this one it would accept a single BLAKE3 pass as proof of work for every header it ever saw. cmd/zycordd selects by this parameter and refuses when the named engine is absent; there is no flag and there will not be one, because a node does not get to choose what it verifies against. An earlier revision of this note claimed the refusal was symmetric. It is not, and a check that fires in a direction where nothing is wrong is noise rather than rigour. See the mainnet note.
notes.randomx_key_interval: Deliberately far smaller than mainnet's 2048/64, so that a devnet crosses key boundaries in minutes rather than in a day and key rotation is exercised by ordinary use instead of by a test that has to be remembered. The ratio is what matters and it is preserved: lag is an eighth of the interval on both networks. See the mainnet note for why the key comes from the height.
notes.max_target: The absolute ceiling on the proof-of-work target (F-PARAM-1); see the mainnet params file for why a purely relative clamp is not a clamp. 2^251 is 8x above the devnet genesis_target of 2^248 and keeps BlockWork at 31: floor(2^256 / (2^251 + 1)) = 31, not 32, because 32 * (2^251 + 1) > 2^256. The headroom is deliberately smaller than mainnet's: a devnet target is already near-trivial, so the room a real chain needs to absorb a hashrate collapse has nowhere to come from and nothing to do. A devnet target is trivial by design, so this bound is exercised rather than relied upon.
notes.future_time_limit_seconds: Identical to mainnet's 180 s, and that is the point of this note: the *rule* is the same and the *exposure* is not. See the mainnet params file for the mechanism. While the controller floored solve times at zero, an attacker dating at now + this - 1 had a fixed point only while its share p < target_block_seconds / future_time_limit_seconds, and devnet's 5 s goal against the same 180 s limit put that at 5/180 = 2.8%, a sixth of mainnet's 16.7%. It compounded with devnet's deliberately small max_target headroom of 8x (mainnet has 4096x), so a ~1% attacker walked a devnet to the ceiling within about ten blocks. THAT IS THE PRE-#30/#96 RULE AND NOT THE SHIPPED ONE: the accumulator is signed and clamped symmetrically (#30) and the retarget normalises against the window average (#96), and sim/timestamp_test.go drives the real rule on devnet params at 1%, 10% and 25% without reaching max_target. What has not changed is the asymmetry this note exists for. Devnet's smaller headroom and faster goal make every timestamp effect proportionally larger here, so a devnet is not a safety model for mainnet on timestamp manipulation; it is the opposite, and it is where an effect is easiest to observe. Measured in sim/timestamp_test.go. See the mainnet note.
notes.min_base_fee: NOT the practical resting point. The base-fee decrease is a proportional step that integer division rounds to zero once the fee falls below base_fee_max_change_denominator, so a quiet chain settles at roughly that denominator rather than here. This matches EIP-1559 and is deterministic. min_base_fee is the hard floor, not the observed one (I1-L3).
notes.par_gas_ratio: The abundant resource: a fixed multiple of the sequential ceiling, so it grows only because that does. Priced cheap, so heavy cryptography does not compete with state mutation.
notes.seq_gas_target_genesis: T₀: the initial value AND the permanent floor of the sequential target T (whitepaper §8.1). Consensus state from block 0, not a constant.
notes.skip_fee: A protocol constant, never a market price (R1-H1). Constancy is what makes the deposit ceiling statelessly checkable — and it is also why applied gas, not included gas, drives the base fees (R2-H2).
notes.ttl_max: Bounds seen-set lifetime (R1-H4) AND the fee-drift window a signer must buffer against (R2-H1). Raising it makes both worse; it is not a free latency knob.
notes.max_sigs_per_block_genesis: The per-block signature ceiling at genesis; see spec/params.json for the derivation. 384 is mainnet's 6000 carried across at devnet's own count ceiling -- 1.5x max_certs_per_block_genesis on both files -- because the ratio is what the number means: 1.5x the honest maximum, which on a count-bound network is one signature per certificate at the count ceiling. Setting devnet to mainnet's 6000 would leave the rule INERT here, since 256 certificates can declare at most 256 x max_sigs = 4,096 signatures, and an inert ceiling reads as covered while covering nothing.
notes.seq_gas_capacity: The ceiling T itself may never pass, and the third structural bound after cert_list_capacity and block_byte_capacity. It exists because clamping only the DERIVED ceilings leaves T free to climb to twice what a full block can hold, where the base-fee target sits above anything a block can deliver and the sequential market stops pricing entirely. Its value is not a free choice: it must preserve the genesis ratio, seq_gas_capacity/seq_gas_target_genesis == block_byte_capacity/block_byte_limit_genesis, so gas and bytes reach their walls together and the terminal state prices exactly like block 0. Validate enforces that as a cross-multiplication.
